implementation_notes: The message is a closed sum type and the router is the visitor: std::visit applies the overload set to whichever alternative the message holds, so adding a message kind without a route fails to compile and no runtime lookup is needed. Destinations are injected into the visitor (a channel/queue reference per arm), and the message is forwarded unchanged. Choose this when the set of routable message types is known at build time - it is the cheapest and the only form the compiler can verify; the route table is not data, so a rule change is a rebuild.
pitfalls: A generic auto-overload (a catch-all) defeats the exhaustiveness guarantee and reintroduces silent misroutes.
The visitor must be callable for every alternative, including cv/ref-qualified ones the forwarding may produce - a missing const& arm is a hard error users meet at the worst time.
valueless_by_exception after a throwing move leaves no alternative to visit.

variants.name: Routing table of std::function handlers
variants.implementation_notes: The open-set form: a route table maps a selector (header value, type tag) to a std::function or function-pointer destination registered at startup or from configuration, and the loop looks the selector up and calls the handler. Prefer it when destinations or rules must change without recompiling, when the message representation is deliberately open, or on a pre-C++17 toolchain; the cost is an erased call per message and a runtime lookup whose miss path must be handled explicitly.
pitfalls: Captured state in the handlers must outlive the router: dangling captures after a rule reload are the classic crash.
An unordered table has unspecified order, so first-match-wins needs an ordered container or an explicit priority.
std::function performs an allocation per stored handler and an indirect call per message - not per-message allocation, but a real cost on hot paths.
